new_statements.quote: Das Nyam ist eine Tonsprache mit zwei phonologisch relevanten Tonebenen, hoch [´] und tief [`]. [p. 44] [...] Ein Zusammenhang von Ton und Druckakzent kann bisher nur an der Oberfläche festgestellt werden. Die möglichen Bedingungen für Akzent könnten in einer Hierarchie wie folgt angeordnet sein: schwere Silben mit Hochton, schwere Silben mit Tiefton und wenn keine schweren Silben vorhanden sind, dann wäre der Akzent mit dem Hochton einer Silbe verknüpft. [fn. 32, p. 50] [...] ‚Akzent‘ bzw. ‚Druckakzent‘ sollte in diesem Zusammenhang zumindest genannt werden. Zum jetzigen Zeitpunkt der Analyse und aufgrund des vorhandenen Materials ist noch keine genauere Beschreibung möglich [fn. 40, p. 60]
new_statements.translation: Nyam is a tone language with two phonologically relevant tone levels, high [´] and low [`]. [...] A connection between tone and stress (Druckakzent) can so far only be established at the surface. The possible conditions for accent could be arranged in a hierarchy as follows: heavy syllables with high tone, heavy syllables with low tone, and if no heavy syllables are present, then the accent would be linked with the high tone of a syllable. [...] 'Accent' or 'stress' should at least be mentioned in this connection. At the present stage of the analysis and given the available material no more precise description is yet possible.
new_statements.citation: Andreas, Heike. 2012. Grammatische Beschreibung des Nyam – eine westtschadische Minoritätensprache. Inauguraldissertation, Fachbereich Sprach- und Kulturwissenschaften, Goethe-Universität Frankfurt am Main (Betreuer Rudolf Leger; Gutachter Rainer Voßen, Herrmann Jungraithmayr).
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (229 pp. DNB deposit copy https://d-nb.info/1044093862/34) opened and read per page with extracted text. All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators: §2.4 Ton, printed p. 44 = PDF p. 53 ("Das Nyam ist eine Tonsprache mit zwei phonologisch relevanten Tonebenen, hoch [´] und tief [`]."); §2.4.2 fn. 32, printed p. 50 = PDF p. 59 (the Ton–Druckakzent hierarchy sentence, word for word); §2.5.2 fn. 40, printed p. 60 = PDF p. 69 (word for word; the reader's quote stops at "möglich" — the sentence continues ", eine solche wird Gegenstand weiterer Forschungen bleiben.", which already gives in full). A grep of the whole text dump for akzent|betonung|betont|stress|promin…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nyam is a two-tone (H/L) language; stress is not part of the phonological description. The author offers only a tentative, explicitly provisional hierarchy for where a phonetic stress/accent would fall: on a heavy (bimoraic: CVV, CVC, CVVC) syllable bearing high tone; failing that on a heavy syllable with low tone; and if the word has no heavy syllable, on a high-toned syllable. I.e. weight-sensitive and tone-attracted, not position-fixed — but the source itself says a proper description is not yet possible.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the whole statement is hedged as a surface observation ('könnten', 'wäre') and fn. 40 says no more precise description is possible on the present material.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (the hierarchy is stated over syllables of the word); no phrase-level accent discussed. Tone chapter treats word and sentence tone patterns separately; tone (not stress) carries lexical and grammatical contrasts. Data from Ndallang consultants (Garba Idi Nyam, Sani Baabale Nyam).
new_statements.identity_note: Same variety as nyam1285: Nyam/Nyambolo of Ndallang (Karim Lamido LGA, Taraba State); the dissertation's two main consultants are from Ndallang. No dialect split is described.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonologie: Nyam is a two-tone language (H, L; p. 44). Stress (Druckakzent) only in two footnotes: fn. 32 p. 50 gives a tentative hierarchy for accent placement (heavy H-toned syllable > heavy L-toned syllable > else the H-toned syllable); fn. 40 p. 60 says no more precise description of accent is yet possible.
Lists only the two descriptive references above; no stress information.
